## Methods

CellScope aims to analyze single-cell data through manifold fitting, enabling precise identification of differences between cell types and subtypes. By identifying highly reliable cliques, the method effectively distinguishes between noise and signal spaces. CellScope then constructs a cell-to-cell similarity graph and performs agglomerative clustering based on this graph to generate a hierarchical structure of cells. A tree-structured visualization intuitively represents the hierarchical relationships and reveals differentiation pathways among cells. Furthermore, CellScope analyzes gene expression changes along differentiation pathways and expression differences within the same hierarchy, providing functional insights into genes.

The CellScope workflow consists of five main steps, as explained in detail below: (A) Manifold fitting stage 1, (B) Manifold fitting stage 2, (C) Graph-based agglomerative clustering, (D) Tree-structured visualization, and (E) Characterization of genes from different categories.

The pseudocode and flowchart of the algorithm can be found in Supplementary Note 1.7 and the tutorial website https://cellscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/, respectively.

We summarize the main notations used in the description of the method as follows: suppose we have a expression counts matrix X={x_i}_{i=1}^N, where each vector x_i corresponds to the expression values [x^{(1)},...,x^{(D)}] of the i-th cell across D genes. We also let G={g_i}_{i=1}^D, where G represents the collection of genes related to X. After manifold fitting stage 1, we obtain Y={y_i}_{i=1}^N, where Y represents the scRNA-seq data after manifold fitting stage 1. Each vector y_i corresponds to the expression values [y^{(1)},...,y^{(D_1)}] of the i-th cell across D_1 selected genes, where D_1 << D. The set of selected genes is denoted as G_1={g_b}_{b=1}^{D_1}, where G_1 \subseteq G. Subsequently, after manifold fitting stage 2, we obtain Z={z_i}_{i=1}^N, where Z represents the fitted scRNA-seq data for subsequent downstream analysis.

Manifold fitting stage 1
Data preprocessing. We applied consistent preprocessing to all single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. First, we normalized each cell’s expression profile, which is a standard procedure prior to downstream analyses. This stage is essential for eliminating differences in total expression levels between cells, which may arise from technical or biological factors. It ensures that highly expressed genes in cells with elevated overall expression do not dominate the dimensionality reduction process, thereby preventing bias in subsequent analyses. Let X_P={x_i}_{i=1}^N denote the preprocessed data, where each vector x_i=[x_i^{(1)},...,x_i^{(D)}] represents the expression values of the i-th cell after preprocessing. The set of genes after preprocessing is denoted as G_e={g_i}_{i=1}^D.

Find highly reliable cliques. We begin this process with Principal Component Analysis (PCA)73, aiming to reduce noise and complexity in the data while retaining the primary sources of variation, thereby clarifying the manifold structure of the data and providing a solid foundation for subsequent manifold exploration. In PCA, we set the target dimensionality to n_1 (defaulting to 100) and apply it to the preprocessed data X_P. This results in a collection of cells represented in a low-dimensional space, denoted as P={p_i}_{i=1}^N, where p_i \in R^{n_1}. We aim to identify highly reliable cliques associated with distinct submanifolds, beginning with the identification of the centers of these submanifolds, referred to as manifold seeds. Inspired by ref. 67, local density reflects the compactness of a cell’s surrounding distribution, while relative distance measures the separation of a cell from other cells with higher density. Manifold seeds tend to exhibit significantly higher values in both metrics. Therefore, we evaluate the potential of each cell p_i to serve as a manifold seed by calculating its local density \rho(p_i) and relative distance \delta(p_i), defined as:

\rho(p_i) = \sum_{j \in N_i} d(p_i, p_j), \delta(p_i) = \min_{j \in N_i, \rho(p_j) > \rho(p_i)} d(p_i, p_j), (1)

where N_i is the set of k nearest neighbors of cell p_i (with k=20 by default), and d(\cdot, \cdot) denotes the distance between two cells, defaulting to Euclidean distance. Next, we compute the composite metric:

\gamma(p_i) = \rho(p_i) \delta(p_i), (2)

and select the cells with the highest \gamma(p_i) values as manifold seeds. Specifically, we choose the top m cells with the largest \gamma(p_i) values as manifold seeds, with m being a predefined hyperparameter which refers to the number of submanifolds hypothesized in advance.

However, since m is related to the number of cell types, an intelligent approach is required to determine the number of manifold seeds when the number of cell types is unknown. We first address the issue of scale differences between \rho and \delta in the calculation of \gamma. Both \rho and \delta are normalized as

\rho'(p_i) = \frac{\rho(p_i) - \min(\rho)}{\max(\rho) - \min(\rho)}, \delta'(p_i) = \frac{\delta(p_i) - \min(\delta)}{\max(\delta) - \min(\delta)}, (3)

where \rho={\rho(p_i)}_{i=1}^N and \delta={\delta(p_i)}_{i=1}^N. Next, we compute a scale-less index by multiplying the two normalized metrics:

\gamma'(p_i) = \delta'(p_i) \cdot \rho'(p_i). (4)

We then sort \gamma'={\gamma'(p_i)}_{i=1}^N in descending order, with \gamma''_j representing the j-th value in the sorted list. To further refine the selection of manifold seeds, we introduce the relative rate of change in \gamma'':

R_j = \begin{cases} \frac{\gamma''_{j+1} - \gamma''_j}{\gamma''_j - \gamma''_{j-1}} & \text{if } 2 \le j \le N-1, \\ \frac{\gamma''_2 - \gamma''_1}{\gamma''_1} & \text{if } j=1, \\ 0 & \text{if } j=N. \end{cases} (5)

Finally, we select the manifold seeds that satisfy the following conditions:

C = {p_i | \rho'(p_i) > \bar{\rho'}, \delta'(p_i) > \bar{\delta'}, \gamma'(p_i) > \bar{\gamma'}, R_{I(p_i)} < \bar{R}}, (6)

where \bar{\cdot} denotes the mean value of the respective set and R={R_i}_{i=1}^N. The index I(p_i) refers to the position of \gamma'(p_i) in \gamma'' after sorting \gamma'. The combined metric-based strategy ensures that the selected manifold seeds possess both high local density and relative distance. The introduction of the relative rate of change further optimizes this selection process, intelligently selecting all high-confidence manifold seeds. Ultimately, we denote the set of selected seeds as C={c_1, \dots, c_m}, where m represents the number of seeds selected.

Given that the identified manifold seeds are highly likely to reside at the centers of their respective submanifolds, the cells in the immediate neighborhood of each seed are assumed to belong to the same class as the seed. Therefore, for each seed c_i, we select its k_1 nearest neighboring cells (with k_1=5 by default), denoted as N_{c_i}. To ensure a high-confidence classification of the sets {N_{c_1}, \dots, N_{c_m}}, we combine the concept of connected components in graphs, and define the following partition:

\begin{cases} N_{c_i} \text{ and } N_{c_j} \text{ belong to different groups; if } N_{c_i} \cap N_{c_j} = \phi, \\ N_{c_i} \text{ and } N_{c_j} \text{ belong to the same group; otherwise,} \end{cases} (7)

for 1 \le i \neq j \le m. The resulting partition of high reliable cliques {N_{c_1}, \dots, N_{c_m}} is recorded as \ell_1.

Signal space identification. Due to the significant variance differences of genes in the signal space, both within and between cell clusters, our goal was to identify genes that exhibit notable expression differences, particularly between different cell types, within highly reliable cliques. To do this, we leveraged the high-confidence labels \ell_1 obtained from these reliable cliques and performed a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA74) on each preprocessed gene g_i \in G_e. For each gene, the corresponding p-value was computed based on its expression across different cell clusters. We then selected the top D_1 genes with the lowest p-values (default: D_1=500), denoted as G_1, as the result of gene selection. Furthermore, we retained the genes from the signal space in X_P, denoted as Y.

Manifold fitting stage 2
To further highlight the true biological signals and better reflect the underlying cellular heterogeneity, we project cells located between submanifolds or near manifold boundaries closer to the centers of their respective submanifolds. This process ensures that the boundaries between submanifolds become clearer after projection. We assume that the density of data points decreases as the distance from the manifold center increases. Therefore, our fitting process focuses on low-density points, as they are more likely to be influenced by noise.

First, we calculate the local density \rho(y_i) for each cell y_i to assess its position within the manifold, using the following formula:

\rho(y_i) = \frac{1}{\sum_{y_j \in N_k(y_i)} d(y_i, y_j)}. (8)

We then select the 5% of cells with the lowest densities to form the set of manifold outliers O. We assume that the closest high-density point to each outlier belong to the same class and is closer to the center of its respective manifold. To achieve this, we adopt the projection estimation method defined by the previous work30: for each outlier y_i \in O, the nearest high-density point is y_b = \text{argmin}_{y_b \in Y} d(y_b, y_i), with \rho(y_b) > \rho(y_i), \forall y_i \in O. (9)

Subsequently, while preserving the relative position between the outlier y_i and y_b, we project y_i closer to the center of the manifold, as given by:

z_i = t y_b + (1-t) y_i, (10)

where t is 0.9 by default. For regular points not identified as outliers, we define their projection as z_i = y_i, if y_i \notin O. The final dataset after the second stage of manifold fitting is represented as Z={z_i}_{i=1}^N.

Graph-based agglomerative clustering
In the field of unsupervised learning, distance matrix-based agglomerative clustering methods have been extensively studied and applied75,76, whereas graph-based clustering aggregation techniques remain relatively under-explored. A similarity graph can capture the local neighborhood relationships between points within a submanifold, reflecting the manifold’s local geometric properties. At the same time, through the construction of neighborhood relationships, the graph can represent the connectivity between different submanifolds. Therefore, after obtaining a clear manifold structure, we begin by using the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) algorithm20 to construct the similarity matrix S={s_{ij}}_{i,j=1}^N. Specifically, for each cell z_i, we determine its k=d\log_2(N)e nearest neighboring cells. We first set the similarity between the cell and cells outside its k nearest neighbors to 0. Next, using a Gaussian kernel function, we compute the local similarity s_{ij} between two cells z_i and z_j:

s_{ij} = \exp \left( - \frac{||z_i - z_j||^2}{\sigma_i^2} \right), (11)

where z_j is in the k nearest neighbors of z_i and ||z_i - z_j|| denotes the Euclidean distance, and \sigma_i is a locally adaptive scale parameter satisfying:

\sum_{j=1}^k \exp \left( - \frac{||z_i - z_j||^2}{\sigma_i^2} \right) = \log_2(k). (12)

To construct a symmetric similarity graph, we define the edge similarity w_{ij} as:

w_{ij} = s_{ij} + s_{ji} - s_{ij} \cdot s_{ji}. (13)

The corresponding symmetric similarity matrix is denoted as W={w_{ij}}_{i,j=1}^N. Finally, using the average linkage method based on pairwise similarities, we systematically merge data points starting with each cell as a separate cluster, and denote the clustering results after K steps as T_K. T_{K+1} merges the two clusters with the highest average similarity, i.e., clusters A_\ell and B_\ell that maximize:

[A_\ell, B_\ell] = \text{argmax}_{A,B \in T_K} \frac{1}{|A||B|} \sum_{a \in A} \sum_{b \in B} w_{ab}. (14)

For exceptionally large datasets (with over 30,000 data points), we employ the following optimization strategy: First, we randomly select a representative subset of 30,000 points from the complete dataset to form subset S_1, while the remaining cells constitute subset S_2. After performing hierarchical clustering on S_1 using the average linkage method to obtain clustering result T_K^0, we analyze the distribution of clusters within the k nearest neighbors (default k=5) of each cell z \in S_2 in S_1 and assign z to the cluster with the highest cell count in its k nearest neighbors.

Tree-structured visualization
To comprehensively and systematically explore cell types and their subtypes, we developed a tree-structured visualization method. First, we applied the UMAP algorithm20 to visualize all cells as the root node. Then, each cluster from T_{N-1} was visualized individually to generate the first layer of child nodes. By comparing the clustering results of T_{N-2} and T_{N-1}, we identified two new subtypes within the cells of the first-layer child nodes and visualized them as the second layer of child nodes. This iterative process was repeated in the same manner, advancing layer by layer.

To clearly illustrate the distribution of each pair of subtypes within their parent nodes, we applied a color-coding scheme to the tree-structured visualization. Specifically, each branch’s outermost nodes were colored first, and the colors of the child nodes were then propagated back to their respective parent nodes. This core visualization method effectively reveals the hierarchical relationships between cell types, illustrating how different populations emerge, differentiate, and specialize over time. The tree-structured visualization automatically generated by CellScope is shown in Supplementary Note 1.9 and the tutorial at https://cellscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/.

Characterization of genes from different categories
After generating the Tree-structured visualization, we quantified the gene expression differences between sibling nodes (sharing the same direct parent node) using the Wasserstein distance. This metric measures the minimal transport cost required to transform one probability distribution into another, providing a robust comparison between gene expression profiles from sibling nodes.

For gene g_i, assume its expression in two sibling nodes is represented by P={p_1, \dots, p_n} and Q={q_1, \dots, q_m}, respectively. First, both expression vectors are sorted in ascending order, yielding the ordered vectors P^0={p_1^0, \dots, p_n^0} and Q^0={q_1^0, \dots, q_m^0}. We then compute the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) for the sorted vectors P^0 and Q^0, as defined by the following equations

F_P(p_i^0) = \frac{i}{n}, i=1,2,...,n, (15)

F_Q(q_j^0) = \frac{j}{m}, j=1,2,...,m. (16)

We then use linear interpolation to align the two CDFs F_P and F_Q onto the same probability space. For a given probability value x \in [0,1], if F_P(p_i^0) < x < F_P(p_{i+1}^0), then F_P^{-1}(x) is calculated as

F_P^{-1}(x) = p_i^0 + \frac{x - F_P(p_i^0)}{F_P(p_{i+1}^0) - F_P(p_i^0)} \cdot (p_{i+1}^0 - p_i^0). (17)

Similarly, F_Q^{-1}(x) is computed in the same manner. Finally, the Wasserstein distance77 is defined as the integral of the absolute difference between the two inverse CDFs across the probability space [0,1]

W_1(P,Q) = \int_0^1 |F_P^{-1}(x) - F_Q^{-1}(x)| dx. (18)

Finally, based on the Wasserstein distance calculated from the expression differences of genes between sibling nodes, we classified the genes into three categories

\begin{cases} \text{Housekeeping gene} & \text{if } W_1(P,Q) < 0.5, \\ \text{Moderately cell-type-related gene} & \text{if } 0.5 \le W_1(P,Q) < 1, \\ \text{Strongly cell-type-related gene} & \text{if } 1 \le W_1(P,Q). \end{cases} (19)

The threshold selection for Wasserstein distance is based on Supplementary Fig. 14, using SubCluster 1 and SubCluster 2 in Siletti-1 (Fig. 4) as an example to demonstrate its rationale. When the Wasserstein distance is less than 0.5, the gene expression distributions are similar. For distances between 0.5 and 1, there are notable differences in means, though some overlap remains, indicating moderate differences in gene expression. When the distance exceeds 1, the first quartile for the cluster with higher mean expression surpasses the third quartile of the other, indicating significant differences in gene expression. In addition, we systematically reviewed three traditional differential gene analysis methods in Supplementary Note 1.6.

If the author aims for CellScope to achieve similar recognition and impact, the following issues may need to be addressed.

Although the author effectively introduces the manifold fitting method in the introduction, it lacks a detailed comparative analysis of its mathematical models against existing frameworks, such as Seurat and Scanpy, particularly in terms of discussing the advantages and limitations of manifold fitting.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript，the authors establish a pipeline, CellScope, to construct high-resolution cell atlases at multiple clustering levels. The pipeline first employs a two-step manifold fitting process to filter out technical noise and housekeeping gene noise from the raw data, followed by agglomerative clustering for precise hierarchical classification. The experiments are detailed, particularly in providing the sources and access links for all benchmark datasets in the Supplementary File, which provides enough detail for reproducing the work. However, there are still some shortcomings that need to be addressed. I have the following questions for the authors:
[comment-1]The manifold fitting method has been proposed and applied to single-cell analysis, as demonstrated in the paper titled "Single-Cell Analysis via Manifold Fitting: A Framework for RNA Clustering and Beyond", published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America (PNAS). What are the differences between the method proposed in this paper and existing methods? What are the innovations? If the manifold fitting method used in proposed method is the same with scAMF, the reference should be clearly marked where the manifold fitting method appears. Also, the difference and relationship should be clearly stated in the paper. Furthermore, the steps of the manifold fitting method should not occupy a significant portion of the text, as this method has already been proposed. Readers can refer to the original text for specific details. The authors should focus on introducing the innovative steps of the proposed method.
[comment-2] In the cell clustering task, the authors compared their method with Scanpy and Seurat. Although Scanpy (2018) and Seurat (2019) are widely used pipelines, there are also many new methods specifically for clustering tasks in recent years. The authors should conduct comparative experiments with these new methods and analyze the results.
[comment-3] In the Runtime Comparison experiments, CellScope demonstrated superior computational efficiency compared to Scanpy and Seurat. However, how does its memory usage compare to these baselines? In single-cell analyses, memory consumption is equally as critical as time efficiency, as it directly impacts the ability of a server to process larger datasets. It is recommended that the authors add an additional row of data in the Table S4, which compares the memory usage of the baselines methods when running on the same dataset.
[comment-4] In the Supplementary File, the background colors of the experimental data in the tables presenting are quite confusing. For instance, in Table S7, the result of 1.00 for Yan of CellScope is highlighted in green, whereas the same value of 1.00 for Siletti-1 of CellScope is marked in light green. • Q9. The paper lacks a detailed discussion on how CellScope addresses the challenges faced by
Seurat and Scanpy in a dialectical manner, particularly the features that Seurat and Scanpy
possess but CellScope currently lacks. Additionally, the author should clearly outline at the
end of the manuscript how CellScope has the potential to become the next leading framework
for single-cell sequencing data analysis.
Response (Bingjie): We have addressed this important question by adding a comprehensive
discussion paragraph at the end of discussion section in our revised manuscript. Here we
quote:
"While CellScope addresses key limitations of established frameworks like Seurat
and Scanpy through its manifold-based gene selection and hierarchical cluster
ing approach, we acknowledge that these established methods possess valuable
features including mature ecosystems, extensive documentation, and broad data
type support that currently exceed CellScope’s scope. Seurat’s modular R-based
architecture and Scanpy’s Python integration offer computational accessibility
and workflow flexibility that have made them community standards. However,
CellScope’s theoretical foundations—particularly its ability to distinguish bio
logical signal from noise and capture cellular hierarchies—position it to become
the next leading framework for single-cell analysis. As datasets grow larger
and more complex, CellScope’s parameter-free operation, superior clustering
performance, and discovery-oriented design address critical needs that existing
methods struggle to meet. Moving forward, we plan to continuously maintain
and enhance the CellScope package, including expanding its compatibility with
emerging data modalities such as spatial transcriptomics and multimodal omics
integration. Additionally, we envision systematic reanalysis of large-scale public
databases using CellScope’s framework, which could reveal previously undetected
cellular subtypes and biological insights across diverse tissues and disease contexts.
Through sustained development, community engagement, and comprehensive
reanalysis efforts, CellScope has the potential to establish itself as the preferred
framework for researchers seeking to push the boundaries of cellular biology
understanding beyond traditional cell type identification toward comprehensive
functional characterization and novel biological discovery."
We acknowledge that established frameworks like Seurat and Scanpy possess significant
advantages that currently exceed CellScope’s scope, including:
– Mature ecosystems with extensive third-party extensions
– Comprehensive documentation and community support
22
– Broad data type compatibility (multimodal, spatial, etc.)
– Established computational accessibility and workflow flexibility
However, CellScope addresses several key limitations of these frameworks through its unique
theoretical foundations:
– Manifold-based gene selection that better distinguishes biological signal from noise
– Hierarchical clustering approach that captures cellular hierarchies more effectively
– Parameter-free operation that reduces user bias and improves reproducibility
– Superior performance on large-scale datasets as demonstrated in our evaluations
Rather than claiming to be the definitive next-generation framework, we position CellScope
as a complementary approach that could potentially fill important gaps in current single-cell
analysis workflows. As datasets become increasingly complex, CellScope’s discovery-oriented
design may offer valuable advantages for researchers seeking to identify novel cellular subtypes
and biological insights.
Our development roadmap includes: (1) expanding compatibility with emerging data modali
ties, (2) systematic reanalysis of public databases to validate broader applicability, and (3)
sustained community engagement to gather feedback and improve functionality. Through
these efforts, CellScope aims to contribute meaningfully to the single-cell analysis ecosystem
rather than replace existing successful frameworks.

The author presents CellScope, an innovative framework for constructing high-resolution cell atlases
at multiple clustering levels. Overall, the paper is innovative, with a reasonable methodology and
sufficient experimental design. The work is promising, as it has the potential to be widely adopted
by researchers, leading to a highly cited paper. However, Seurat and Scanpy are currently well-
established analytical frameworks. If the author aims for CellScope to achieve similar recognition
and impact, the following issues may need to be addressed.
Major Points
• Q1. The manifold fitting method has been proposed and applied to single-cell analysis, as
demonstrated in the paper titled “Single-Cell Analysis via Manifold Fitting: A Framework
for RNA Clustering and Beyond”, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of
Sciences of the United States of America (PNAS). What are the differences between the
method proposed in this paper and existing methods? What are the innovations? If the
manifold fitting method used in the proposed method is the same as scAMF, the reference
should be clearly marked where the manifold fitting method appears. Also, the difference and
relationship should be clearly stated in the paper. Furthermore, the steps of the manifold
fitting method should not occupy a significant portion of the text, as this method has already
been proposed. Readers can refer to the original text for specific details. The authors should
focus on introducing the innovative steps of the proposed method.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important question regarding the relationship
between our proposed CellScope method and existing manifold fitting approaches, particularly
scAMF.Intherevisedmanuscript,wehaveaddedclearreferencestoscAMFwherevermanifold
fitting is mentioned, and explicitly stated the conceptual relationship and practical differences
between the two methods (Page 5, line 129–137 in the manuscript, and supplementary
Note 1.2), and focused our methodology description on CellScope’s innovative components
rather than general manifold fitting principles.
Manifold fitting represents a broad conceptual framework or theoretical paradigm for dimen-
sionality reduction that aims to preserve data structure while offering high interpretability.
Based on this conceptual foundation, multiple distinct and operationally different models can
be independently developed to achieve specific analytical goals. Both scAMF and CellScope
are concrete implementations that draw from this manifold fitting concept but represent
fundamentally different mathematical models designed independently to address distinct
1
biological challenges.
As detailed in our revised manuscript and supplementary, and summarized in Table R1,
while CellScope and scAMF share the conceptual foundation of manifold fitting, their specific
implementations are fundamentally distinct across multiple key technical aspects:
1. Theoretical Foundation: scAMF employs a general manifold hypothesis for noise
reduction, whereas CellScope introduces a biology-driven dual-noise model that explicitly
distinguishes housekeeping gene noise from technical noise with explicit biological noise
characterization.
2. Manifold Identification: CellScope implements two-step biological manifold fitting
with cell-type-aware submanifold detection, contrasting with scAMF’s single adaptive
manifold fitting approach.
3. Manifold Seeds Selection: CellScopeemployscompositemetrics(ρ×δ)withbiological
validation for cell-type center identification, while scAMF lacks this dedicated module.
4. Projection Strategy: CellScope implements two-stage projection comprising signal
space identification and boundary cell refinement through sequential biological and
technical denoising, compared to scAMF’s maximum density point along projection line
approach.

• Q6. The challenges addressed by this work should be explained in Introduction Section in
details with examples.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. Following the reviewer’s
recommendation, we have added a comprehensive description of three key challenges that
CellScope addresses in single-cell analysis:
1. Gene Selection and Characterization Limitations: Current methods suffer from
inadequate and inaccurate gene selection coupled with single-level marker gene char
acterization that fails to dynamically capture genes along cell type subdivisions. This
limitation prevents researchers from identifying cell-type-specific markers that change
across different levels of cellular hierarchy.
2. Clustering Resolution and Structure Deficiencies: Existing approaches provide
limited clustering resolution and hierarchical structure that cannot achieve nested
organization, making it difficult to capture the full spectrum of cellular diversity and
relationships.
3. Visualization Integration Challenges: Current methods lack the ability to generate
tree-structured visualizations that integrate cellular trees with cellular atlases, limiting
comprehensive understanding of cellular organization.
To address these challenges, we have clearly outlined CellScope’s four core innovations:
– Intelligent gene selection that separates signal from noise spaces
– Precise delineation of similar cell subpopulations through manifold-based denoising
– Dynamic characterization of cellular landscapes at multiple resolutions
– Multi-level functional analysis through dynamic molecular identity classification
We have also included specific examples of CellScope’s achievements that demonstrate these
capabilities:
– Identification of novel oligodendrocyte subpopulations that existing methods failed to
detect
– Simultaneous detection of cell types and health status in COVID-19 patients
– Superior performance across 36 diverse datasets covering various species, organs, and
sequencing modalities

• Q7. To our knowledge, agglomerative clustering has a high computational complexity and is
not suitable for large-scale data. The authors should analyze the complexity of hierarchical
clustering and conduct experiments on large-scale datasets to analyze its performance.
Response: While the naive agglomerative clustering algorithm exhibits a worst-case time
complexity of O(N3), we have implemented two key optimizations to make it tractable for
large-scale single-cell datasets:
– Optimized linkage via fastcluster: By leveraging the highly efficient Python package
fastcluster [4], we reduce the clustering step to the theoretically optimal O(N2) bound.
– Subsampling with efficient assignment: We randomly select a fixed subset of 30,000
cells and build the full adjacency matrix only for this subset—thereby bounding the
worst-case complexity to O(30,0002)—and then assign the remaining cells to clusters
using nearest neighbor assignment in linear time. The subset size of 30,000 cells is
adjustable based on available computational memory and time requirements, providing
flexibility for different hardware configurations.
To address concerns about representativeness, our extensive validation on large-scale datasets
demonstrates that 30,000 cells provide sufficient representation of the entire dataset structure.
The un-sampled cells are assigned to clusters through nearest neighbor identification to the
sampled cells, ensuring comprehensive coverage while maintaining computational efficiency.
Our clustering and visualization results on large-scale datasets confirm that this subsampling
strategy achieves excellent clustering accuracy and enables meaningful biological discoveries
without compromising the detection of rare cell types or subtle cellular relationships.

• Q8. Is the agglomerative clustering method used in the proposed approach original or pre
existing? If it is pre-existing, the authors should clearly indicate the references and provide
an explanation.
Response: Distance matrix-based agglomerative clustering methods have been extensively
studied and applied in numerous works [5, 7]. These existing classical methods have been
referenced in the manuscript. CellScope innovatively incorporates UMAP graph structures
into the agglomerative clustering process, which is a new method. This unique design enables
the algorithm to simultaneously achieve precise modeling of local manifold structures and
preservation of global topological properties, thereby effectively capturing cellular neigh
borhood relationships within submanifolds while accurately identifying spatial correlations
between different submanifolds. Specifically, our agglomerative clustering module integrates
the following core components:
– Novel similarity graph construction: We introduce a new approach to build the similarity
matrix S by capturing local neighborhood relationships within each learned submani
fold. This construction encodes both the manifold’s intrinsic geometric structure and
the connectivity across submanifolds. Specifically, we employ the Uniform Manifold
Approximation and Projection (UMAP) algorithm to compute pairwise affinities and
generate S. Full algorithmic details are provided in the Methods section. As shown in
Figure 6, our graph-based approach outperforms traditional distance-based matrices in
clustering performance.
– Classical agglomerative clustering: After constructing the similarity matrix S, we
perform agglomerative clustering through an iterative merging strategy: sequentially
combining the two clusters with the highest average similarity at each step until only
two cluster structures remain.

• Q3. I suggest including pseudo-code and flowcharts to further improve the readability and
clarity of the proposed method.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions aimed at improving the readability and clarity of
our method. In response, we have provided a detailed algorithmic flowchart of the CellScope
workflow as Algorithm 1 (corresponded to Supplementary Algorithm 1), which clearly
outlines the five core computational steps—Manifold Fitting Stage 1, Manifold Fitting Stage
2, Hierarchical Clustering, Tree-Structured Visualization, and Gene Characterization—along
with the default hyperparameters used at each stage. Additionally, we have included a compre
hensive textual description of the workflow as Figure R1(corresponded to Supplementary
Figure S1) to further enhance reproducibility and clarity.
The overall computational procedure consists of the following key stages:
1. Manifold Fitting Stage 1: The raw gene expression data is first log-transformed and
row-normalized. Dimensionality is then reduced to 100 via PCA. Based on the reduced
dimensions, the local density and relative distance of cells are computed. The top 500
genes with the smallest p-values are selected as high-confidence seed genes. Feature
genes are further refined through ANOVA-based differential analysis across pre-labeled
cell cliques.
2. Manifold Fitting Stage 2: Cells within the lowest 5% of density values are identified
as outliers. Their positions are adjusted by 90% toward their nearest neighboring cells
to enhance the continuity and topological stability of the underlying manifold. The
outcome of this stage is the fitted data.
3. Similarity Graph Construction and Clustering: A cell-specific similarity graph is built
following the UMAP algorithm. Hierarchical clustering is then applied to this graph to
identify distinct cell subpopulations.
4. Downstream Analysis: This final phase encompasses three main tasks: (a) constructing
tree-structured visualizations to illustrate developmental trajectories; (b) detecting
marker genes for each identified cell cluster; and (c) categorizing genes based on their
expression dynamics using Wasserstein distance.
For user convenience, we have also provided a detailed text-based workflow diagram in the
online tutorial, available at https://cellscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/, to facilitate
better learning and understanding. We believe these supplementary materials effectively
enhance the transparency of the methodology and make the research outcomes easier to
reproduce.

• Q4. I suggest adding comparative analysis with the following method, "scCRT: a contrastive-
based dimensionality reduction model for scRNA-seq trajectory inference".
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion regarding scCRT [1]. scCRT is a
dimensionality reduction framework specifically designed for trajectory inference that does
not include a clustering pipeline, unlike CellScope, Seurat, or Scanpy. Additionally, scCRT
partially utilizes label information during training, which would make direct unsupervised
clustering comparisons less fair. Therefore, we did not directly compare scCRT’s clustering
performance with other algorithms in our main analysis. Instead, we added a comparative
description of this framework in our discussion, highlighting its capability in applying
dimensionalityreductionfortrajectoryinference: "RecentmethodssuchasscCRT[1]represent
another crucial approach to single-cell analysis, which innovatively combines cell-level pairwise
modules with cluster-level contrastive learning to preserve cellular relationships for trajectory
inference applications. While both scCRT and CellScope learn highly informative low-
dimensional representations and leverage clustering information, they differ in their design
focus: scCRT emphasizes continuous processes and trajectory analysis, whereas CellScope is
optimized for discrete clustering tasks and multi-resolution cellular characterization."
Based on our curiosity, we conducted a special experiment using scCRT features as input
to CellScope and Scanpy. As shown in Table R3, CellScope achieves superior clustering
accuracy on most datasets with an average ARI of 0.88, compared to 0.81 for scCRT
features combined with CellScope clustering. For Scanpy, scCRT features provide moderate
improvements, increasing the average ARI from 0.68 (Scanpy alone) to 0.74 (scCRT features
+ Scanpy clustering) across 17 datasets. However, the scCRT-enhanced Scanpy still performs
less effectively than CellScope for clustering tasks. These results demonstrate that scCRT
embeddings can enhance existing clustering methods, while CellScope remains more effective
for discrete clustering applications.
